# Machine-Learned Noise Models for Quantum Error Mitigation on NISQ Processors

## 1. Background and motivation

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors now offer between 50 and a few
hundred qubits, but they remain limited by decoherence, gate infidelity, readout error,
and crosstalk. Without full fault-tolerant error correction, which demands physical
qubit counts and gate fidelities still out of reach, the near-term path to useful
computation runs through error *mitigation* rather than error *correction*. Error
mitigation accepts that the hardware is noisy and instead post-processes results, or
adjusts circuits, so that expectation values approach their noise-free counterparts.

Two mitigation techniques dominate current practice. Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE)
runs a circuit at several artificially amplified noise levels and extrapolates the
measured expectation value back to the zero-noise limit. Probabilistic error
cancellation (PEC) represents the inverse of the noise channel as a quasi-probability
distribution over implementable operations, then samples from it so that the averaged
result is unbiased. Both methods share a single structural dependency: they need a model
of the device noise. ZNE needs to know how noise scales when it is amplified; PEC needs
an explicit characterisation of each noisy gate so that its inverse can be constructed.

The accuracy of mitigation is therefore bounded by the accuracy of the noise model.
Today most deployments use a simple noise model, typically a depolarising or Pauli
channel fitted to a handful of randomised-benchmarking numbers, or a sparse model
calibrated through gate-set tomography on one or two qubits. These models are cheap but
crude. They assume noise is local, Markovian, time-stationary, and independent across
qubits. Real devices violate every one of those assumptions. Crosstalk couples
spatially separated gates, control electronics drift over minutes to hours, and
non-Markovian memory effects appear in superconducting and trapped-ion platforms alike.
When the model is wrong, PEC produces biased estimates and ZNE extrapolates along the
wrong curve.

This proposal asks whether a machine-learned noise model, trained directly on device
measurements, can capture the spatial and temporal structure that hand-built models
miss, and whether feeding such a model into PEC and ZNE measurably improves mitigated
expectation values on real NISQ hardware. The central idea is not to replace the
physics but to let a flexible function approximator absorb the residual structure that
the physics-based model leaves on the table.

## 2. Hypothesis and research questions

**Primary hypothesis.** A noise model parameterised by a neural network and trained on
randomised-circuit measurements will predict device error channels more accurately than
a standard sparse Pauli-Lindblad baseline, and substituting it into PEC will reduce the
bias of mitigated expectation values on a 27-qubit superconducting processor by a factor
of at least two at fixed sampling cost, for circuits up to depth 40.

We decompose this into four research questions.

**RQ1.** Can a learned model predict held-out error rates (for gate combinations and
qubit subsets not seen during training) more accurately than the Pauli-Lindblad
baseline, measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence on a tomographically characterised
test set?

**RQ2.** Does the learned model recover known crosstalk and drift structure that the
baseline ignores, and can we attribute its predictions to physically interpretable terms
through an ablation of its input features?

**RQ3.** When the learned model is plugged into PEC and ZNE, does the bias of mitigated
expectation values fall, and by how much, relative to the same protocols using the
baseline model, at matched shot budgets?

**RQ4.** How does the advantage scale with circuit depth and qubit number, and at what
point does the sampling overhead of PEC erase the benefit?

Stating the hypothesis quantitatively, with a fixed sampling budget and a defined
circuit family, makes the project falsifiable. If the learned model fails to beat the
baseline on RQ1, the downstream questions become moot, and we report that cleanly.

## 3. Related work and positioning

Gate-set tomography gives an exhaustive characterisation of a small qubit register but
scales exponentially and cannot cover a full device. Randomised benchmarking and its
variants give scalable but coarse summaries, typically a single average error rate per
gate. Sparse Pauli-Lindblad models, which underpin recent large-scale PEC demonstrations,
strike a balance: they assume the generator of the noise channel is a sum of a tractable
number of Pauli terms whose rates are learned from cycle benchmarking. This is the
state-of-the-art baseline we target, and we deliberately do not strawman it.

Machine learning has been applied to quantum control, to readout-error classification,
and to learning syndrome decoders for error-corrected codes. Our contribution sits in a
less crowded space: learning the *generator* of a continuous noise channel for the
explicit purpose of inverting it inside a mitigation protocol. The closest prior work
treats the noise model as a black box that predicts corrected expectation values
directly, skipping the channel. We argue that learning the channel, rather than the
corrected output, keeps the method compatible with the unbiasedness guarantee of PEC and
yields an interpretable object that can be audited against physics. That interpretability
is a design choice with a cost, discussed in the risks section.

## 4. Methods

### 4.1 Hardware and platform

The primary platform is a 27-qubit fixed-frequency transmon device accessed through a
cloud provider, with calibration data exposed per job. We will also run a subset of
experiments on a trapped-ion device with all-to-all connectivity to test whether
conclusions transfer across hardware with different dominant noise mechanisms. Using two
physically distinct platforms guards against a result that is really a quirk of one
device.

### 4.2 Data collection

Training data comes from randomised circuits in the mirror-circuit family, where the
ideal output is known by construction, so any deviation is attributable to noise. For
each circuit we record the full measured bitstring distribution over many shots, along
with the device calibration metadata at execution time: per-qubit T1 and T2, single- and
two-qubit gate errors, readout assignment matrices, and timestamps. We will collect data
across several weeks to capture drift, and we will interleave circuits spatially to
sample crosstalk between many qubit pairs. Each record is therefore a (circuit,
calibration context, measured distribution) triple.

### 4.3 Model architecture

The learned model predicts the rates of a Pauli-Lindblad generator, but instead of one
fitted rate per term it outputs the rates as a function of context. The architecture is a
graph neural network whose nodes are qubits and whose edges follow the device coupling
map. Node and edge features include the calibration metadata, the gates scheduled in the
current layer, and the gates scheduled in neighbouring sites (to expose crosstalk). The
network outputs a vector of Pauli-Lindblad rates for the layer. By embedding the output
in the same Pauli-Lindblad form as the baseline, we keep the channel physically
well-formed (completely positive and trace preserving) and directly invertible for PEC.

This is a deliberate constraint. A fully unconstrained network could fit the training
distributions better but might output non-physical channels that PEC cannot invert. We
trade a little expressivity for a guarantee that the learned object is usable downstream.

### 4.4 Training objective

The model is trained to minimise the divergence between the distribution it predicts
(obtained by simulating the noisy circuit under the model-output channel) and the
measured distribution. Because simulating the noisy circuit exactly is expensive, we use
circuits in a Clifford-dominated regime where efficient classical simulation of the
noisy dynamics is tractable, supplemented by a smaller set of near-Clifford circuits
evaluated with tensor-network methods. We regularise toward the baseline model so that,
in the low-data limit, the learned model degrades gracefully to the established
state-of-the-art rather than to noise.

### 4.5 Integration into mitigation

For PEC, the learned channel is inverted per layer to produce the quasi-probability
decomposition, exactly as in the baseline pipeline but with context-dependent rates. For
ZNE, we use the learned model to choose noise-amplification factors and to inform the
extrapolation functional form, replacing the usual assumption of a fixed polynomial. In
both cases the mitigation algorithm is unchanged; only the noise model feeding it is
swapped, which isolates the contribution of the model itself.

### 4.6 Sampling-cost accounting

PEC pays for unbiasedness with a sampling overhead that grows exponentially in the total
error rate of the circuit. A noise model that is more accurate but implies a larger
quasi-probability norm could, in principle, raise that overhead even as it lowers bias.
Any honest comparison must therefore hold the shot budget fixed and report bias at equal
cost, not bias alone. We define the comparison precisely: for each benchmark circuit we
allocate an identical total number of shots to the baseline pipeline and to the learned
pipeline, distribute those shots according to each method's own sampling distribution, and
compare the resulting bias and variance of the mitigated estimator. If the learned model
lowers bias only by spending more shots, that is not an improvement, and our accounting
will surface it rather than hide it. We will also report the sampling overhead itself as a
function of depth, since a model that improves accuracy but blows up the overhead is of
limited practical use.

### 4.7 Avoiding leakage between training and evaluation

A subtle failure mode is data leakage: if the circuits, qubit subsets, or calibration
epochs used to train the model overlap with those used to evaluate it, the reported
advantage is inflated. We enforce three separations. First, circuit-structure separation:
the evaluation circuits come from a circuit family disjoint from the training family.
Second, spatial separation: a subset of qubit pairs is held out entirely from training so
that crosstalk generalisation can be tested on unseen geometry. Third, temporal
separation: evaluation uses calibration epochs that postdate the training window, which
tests whether the model truly conditions on current device state rather than memorising a
snapshot. Only results that survive all three separations count toward the headline claim.

## 5. Evaluation plan

We evaluate at three levels.

**Model level (RQ1, RQ2).** On a held-out set of tomographically characterised gate
sequences and qubit subsets, we compare the learned model and the baseline by KL
divergence and by total-variation distance between predicted and measured distributions.
For RQ2 we ablate input features (removing neighbour-gate features, removing timestamps)
and check whether crosstalk and drift signatures vanish, which would confirm the model is
using that information rather than overfitting.

**Mitigation level (RQ3).** On benchmark circuits with classically computable ideal
expectation values (for example Trotterised transverse-field Ising dynamics in regimes
still simulable), we measure the bias of mitigated estimates under the learned model
versus the baseline, at matched shot budgets. The headline metric is the ratio of
absolute biases. We pre-register a target of at least a two-fold bias reduction at depth
40 and will report the result whether or not it is met.

**Scaling level (RQ4).** We sweep circuit depth and the number of active qubits and plot
bias and sampling overhead jointly, locating the crossover depth beyond which PEC's
overhead makes the learned model's advantage uneconomical.

Crucially, every comparison holds the mitigation algorithm and the shot budget fixed and
varies only the noise model. We will report negative and partial results, and we will
release the trained model, the circuit sets, and the analysis code so that others can
reproduce and contest the findings.

## 6. Risks and mitigations

**Risk: the learned model overfits to a particular calibration epoch.** Device drift
means a model trained this week may be stale next week. Mitigation: we include
timestamped calibration data as input so the model conditions on the current device
state rather than memorising one snapshot, and we test on data from epochs held out in
time, not just held out by circuit.

**Risk: classical simulability of the training circuits limits the regime we can train
in.** Our training objective needs a classically computable reference, which confines us
to Clifford-dominated and near-Clifford circuits. The learned model may not extrapolate
to deeply non-Clifford regimes. Mitigation: we characterise this limit explicitly,
quantify how performance degrades as circuits move away from the Clifford regime, and are
candid that the method inherits the simulability frontier as a hard boundary.

**Risk: the interpretability constraint costs accuracy.** By forcing the output into a
Pauli-Lindblad form we may leave structure uncaptured. Mitigation: we run an
unconstrained-model arm purely as a diagnostic upper bound on achievable fit, not for
deployment, so we know how much accuracy the constraint costs.

**Risk: the two-fold target is missed.** The pre-registered threshold may not be reached.
This is a scientific outcome, not a failure of execution, and the proposal is structured
so that a null result on RQ3 is still informative about the limits of model-based
mitigation.

The project runs over 24 months.

  baseline on both platforms; reproduce published PEC results as a sanity check.
- **Months 5 to 10.** Develop and train the graph-network noise model; complete RQ1 and

- **Months 11 to 16.** Integrate the learned model into PEC and ZNE; run RQ3 mitigation

competitors should be able to take the released materials and either reproduce our central

far more credible than one tuned to a lucky day on the machine.

If the central hypothesis holds, the immediate consequence is practical: existing PEC and
ZNE deployments could improve their accuracy at no extra sampling cost simply by swapping

unchanged. The longer-term significance is methodological. It would establish that the
residual structure left behind by physics-based noise models, crosstalk, drift, and weak
non-Markovian memory, is both real and learnable, and that capturing it pays off
downstream. That would reframe noise characterisation as a learning problem with a clear
objective rather than a one-off calibration exercise.

If the hypothesis fails, the contribution is still substantive. A clean negative result,
that a flexible learned model trained on rich calibration context cannot beat a sparse
Pauli-Lindblad baseline inside PEC, would tell the field that the baseline already
captures the mitigation-relevant structure and that effort is better spent elsewhere, for
example on reducing the sampling overhead of PEC rather than on refining the noise model.
Either way the controlled design converts the question into evidence.

## 10. Expected contributions

The project will deliver (i) an open dataset of randomised-circuit measurements with rich
calibration context across two hardware platforms, (ii) a context-dependent,
physically constrained learned noise model with an audited account of what structure it
captures, (iii) a controlled measurement of how much such a model improves PEC and ZNE
at fixed cost, and (iv) an honest map of the regimes where the approach helps and where
its overhead or simulability constraints make it uneconomical. Whether the headline
hypothesis holds or not, the controlled design ensures the result advances understanding
of model-limited error mitigation on NISQ hardware.

# Why History Proves That Technology Has Always Made Humanity Happier

## Introduction

There is no clearer lesson in the whole of human history than this: every time we have
invented a new technology, we have become happier. From the first sharpened flint to the
smartphone in your pocket, the arc of progress bends in a single, unmistakable direction,
upward, toward greater ease, greater comfort, and greater joy. To doubt this is to doubt
history itself. The evidence is everywhere, written into the rising tide of human
flourishing that technology has carried on its back since the dawn of our species. In the
pages that follow I will show, decisively, that technology has always made humanity
happier, and that it always will.

## The deep past: fire, farming, and the first happiness

Consider our earliest ancestors. Before they learned to make fire, they huddled in the
cold and the dark, miserable and afraid. Then came fire, and with it warmth, cooked food,
and light against the night. Who could deny that this made them happier? The discovery of
fire is the first proof of our thesis: a technology arrived, and human life improved.

The same is true of agriculture. When our ancestors learned to farm, they no longer had
to wander hungrily across the land in search of food. They settled down, built villages,
and enjoyed the security of a reliable harvest. The invention of farming gave us
civilisation itself, and civilisation is plainly a happier state than the brutish
struggle that preceded it. Every farmer who watched his crops ripen felt a contentment
his wandering ancestors never knew.

From fire and farming flow all the comforts we cherish. The pattern is set at the very
beginning of our story, and it never breaks: technology comes, and happiness follows.

## The wheel, the plough, and the rising tide

The wheel is another perfect illustration. Before the wheel, people carried everything on
their backs, bent double under their burdens. After the wheel, they rolled their goods to
market with ease and smiles on their faces. Every cart that ever creaked down a country
lane was a little engine of happiness, sparing human muscles and gladdening human hearts.

# The Gut Microbiome and Mental Health: A Critical Review of the Gut-Brain Axis

## Abstract

Over the past two decades, the idea that intestinal microbes influence mood, cognition and behaviour has moved from the margins of microbiology to a busy crossroads of neuroscience, gastroenterology and psychiatry. This review surveys the evidence linking the gut microbiome to mental health, with particular attention to the so-called gut-brain axis. We summarise the mechanistic pathways proposed to connect the two organs, the animal experiments that established the field, and the human observational and interventional studies that have followed. Throughout, we distinguish correlation from causation, flag methodological weaknesses, and identify the open questions that the field has yet to resolve. Our overall assessment is cautiously optimistic but deliberately restrained: the animal evidence is strong and mechanistically rich, the human evidence is suggestive but largely correlational, and the clinical promise of microbiome-targeted psychiatric treatment remains unproven.

## 1. Introduction

The human gastrointestinal tract harbours a community of microorganisms numbering in the tens of trillions, dominated by bacteria but also including archaea, fungi and viruses. Collectively termed the gut microbiota, and together with their genes the gut microbiome, this community participates in digestion, immune development, vitamin synthesis and the metabolism of drugs and dietary compounds. A growing body of work proposes that it also communicates with the central nervous system, forming a bidirectional signalling network commonly called the gut-brain axis.

The clinical motivation is plain. Depression and anxiety disorders are among the leading causes of disability worldwide, and existing treatments help only a fraction of patients into full remission. If gut microbes shape mood, then diet, probiotics or faecal transplantation might offer new and relatively low-risk avenues for intervention. The scientific motivation is equally compelling: the microbiome offers a tractable, modifiable variable through which environment, diet and host genetics might jointly influence the brain.

This review has three aims. First, to lay out the proposed mechanisms of gut-brain communication. Second, to weigh the animal and human evidence separately, because they differ sharply in strength. Third, to be candid about what we do not yet know. We have tried to avoid the two failure modes that dog this literature: uncritical enthusiasm, which treats every correlation as a breakthrough, and reflexive dismissal, which ignores a genuinely interesting and reproducible set of animal findings.

## 2. Mechanisms of gut-brain communication

Several plausible and partly overlapping pathways could allow gut microbes to influence the brain.

### 2.1 The vagus nerve

The vagus nerve is the principal parasympathetic conduit between the gut and the brainstem. A frequently cited experiment showed that the anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects of a particular Lactobacillus strain in mice disappeared when the vagus nerve was severed, implicating direct neural signalling. The vagal route is attractive because it is fast and anatomically direct, but it is unlikely to be the whole story, since several microbial effects persist after vagotomy.

### 2.2 Microbial metabolites

Gut bacteria ferment dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids, principally acetate, propionate and butyrate. These molecules influence the integrity of the gut epithelium and the blood-brain barrier, modulate microglial maturation, and act as signalling molecules in their own right. Butyrate in particular is a histone deacetylase inhibitor and can alter gene expression in host cells. Microbes also produce or modulate neuroactive compounds, including gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and they influence host serotonin. It is worth stressing that although the vast majority of the body's serotonin is produced in the gut, this peripheral serotonin does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so the popular claim that gut bacteria supply the brain with serotonin is at best an oversimplification.

### 2.3 The immune system and inflammation

The gut is the body's largest immune organ, and the microbiota calibrates immune development from birth. Dysbiosis, meaning a disturbed microbial community, can increase intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation. Because inflammation is itself associated with depression in a subset of patients, the immune route offers a mechanistically coherent link between gut state and mood. The difficulty is directionality: stress and depression also alter gut physiology and immune function, so inflammation may be cause, consequence or both.

### 2.4 The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

The HPA axis governs the body's stress response. Germ-free animals, raised without any microbes, show an exaggerated HPA response to stress, which can be partially normalised by colonisation early in life. This suggests that microbial exposure during a developmental window helps to set the calibration of the stress system, an observation with obvious relevance to mood disorders.

These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, and the most credible models invoke several acting together. Importantly, demonstrating that a pathway can carry a signal is not the same as showing that it does so in humans under ordinary conditions, a distinction we return to repeatedly.

## 3. Evidence from animal models

The animal literature is the strongest part of the field, and it is where causal claims are best supported.

### 3.1 Germ-free animals

Mice raised in sterile isolators provide the clearest causal handle. Compared with conventionally colonised animals, germ-free mice show altered anxiety-like behaviour, changes in the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in regions relevant to mood and memory, and the exaggerated stress response noted above. Crucially, some of these differences can be reversed by colonisation, and the reversal is often time-limited to early life, pointing to a developmental window. Because the only manipulated variable is the presence or absence of microbes, these experiments support a genuinely causal interpretation, at least within the model.

### 3.2 Antibiotic and probiotic manipulations

Disrupting the microbiota with antibiotics, or supplementing specific strains, changes behaviour in rodents in directions broadly consistent with the germ-free work. Administration of particular Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains has reduced anxiety-like and despair-like behaviour in standard rodent assays, sometimes with measurable changes in central GABA receptor expression.

### 3.3 Faecal transplantation across phenotypes

Perhaps the most striking experiments transfer microbiota between animals of differing temperament. Transplanting the microbiota of a bold mouse strain into a timid one, and vice versa, can transfer aspects of the behavioural phenotype along with the microbes. More provocatively, several groups report that transplanting faecal microbiota from humans with depression into rodents induces depression-like and anxiety-like behaviour in the recipients. If robust, this is close to a demonstration of sufficiency: the microbial community alone can carry a behaviourally relevant signal.

### 3.4 Limits of the animal evidence

These findings are genuinely impressive, but three cautions apply. First, rodent assays of anxiety and despair, such as the forced swim test and the elevated plus maze, are imperfect proxies for human mood disorders, and their interpretation is contested even within behavioural neuroscience. Several plausible and partly overlapping pathways could allow gut microbes to influence the brain.

The vagus nerve is the principal parasympathetic conduit between the gut and the brainstem. A frequently cited experiment showed that the anxiolytic and antidepressant-like effects of a particular Lactobacillus strain in mice disappeared when the vagus nerve was severed, implicating direct neural signalling. The vagal route is attractive because it is fast and anatomically direct, but it is unlikely to be the whole story, since several microbial effects persist after vagotomy.

Gut bacteria ferment dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids, principally acetate, propionate and butyrate. These molecules influence the integrity of the gut epithelium and the blood-brain barrier, modulate microglial maturation, and act as signalling molecules in their own right. The difficulty is directionality: stress and depression also alter gut physiology and immune function, so inflammation may be cause, consequence or both.

The HPA axis governs the body's stress response. Germ-free animals, raised without any microbes, show an exaggerated HPA response to stress, which can be partially normalised by colonisation early in life. This suggests that microbial exposure during a developmental window helps to set the calibration of the stress system, an observation with obvious relevance to mood disorders.

The animal literature is the strongest part of the field, and it is where causal claims are best supported.

Crucially, some of these differences can be reversed by colonisation, and the reversal is often time-limited to early life, pointing to a developmental window. ### 3.2 Antibiotic and probiotic manipulations

Disrupting the microbiota with antibiotics, or supplementing specific strains, changes behaviour in rodents in directions broadly consistent with the germ-free work. Administration of particular Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains has reduced anxiety-like and despair-like behaviour in standard rodent assays, sometimes with measurable changes in central GABA receptor expression.

Perhaps the most striking experiments transfer microbiota between animals of differing temperament. Early-life factors, including mode of birth delivery, breastfeeding and antibiotic exposure in infancy, shape the developing microbiome during the very window that animal work suggests is critical for calibrating the stress system. The honest reading is that diet and lifestyle clearly matter for mental health and clearly shape the microbiome, but that the microbiome's role as a mediator of those effects in humans is hypothesised rather than established.

It can also feed a reductive narrative in which complex, multifactorial conditions are recast as simple deficiencies to be corrected with a supplement. A balanced field must hold the biological interest of the microbiome alongside a clear-eyed view of its current clinical limits and the social meanings that attach to it.

## 9. Conclusion

The gut-brain axis is a real and mechanistically rich phenomenon in animal models, where gut microbes demonstrably influence brain chemistry and behaviour. Several plausible and partly overlapping pathways could allow gut microbes to influence the brain.

The vagus nerve is the principal parasympathetic conduit between the gut and the brainstem. These associations are biologically interesting, but they form a dense web of mutual influence in which isolating the microbiome's specific contribution is extraordinarily difficult. The honest reading is that diet and lifestyle clearly matter for mental health and clearly shape the microbiome, but that the microbiome's role as a mediator of those effects in humans is hypothesised rather than established.

The clinical translation of microbiome science carries risks that deserve explicit attention. The most immediate is the gap between public enthusiasm and evidence. Direct-to-consumer microbiome testing services often return reports with confident dietary or supplement recommendations that the underlying science cannot support. Faecal microbiota transplantation illustrates the same tension acutely. It is a genuinely effective therapy for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, which has created a halo effect around the procedure for other indications. For psychiatric conditions, however, the evidence consists of small, mostly uncontrolled studies, and the procedure carries real risks, including the transmission of pathogens, as fatal cases of transmitted infection have shown. Promoting it for depression or anxiety on the current evidence would be premature and potentially dangerous.

There are also conceptual hazards. The framing of mental illness as a problem of gut microbes can subtly shift responsibility onto the individual's diet and lifestyle, echoing older and discredited tendencies to moralise psychiatric illness. It can also feed a reductive narrative in which complex, multifactorial conditions are recast as simple deficiencies to be corrected with a supplement. A balanced field must hold the biological interest of the microbiome alongside a clear-eyed view of its current clinical limits and the social meanings that attach to it.

## 9. Conclusion

The gut-brain axis is a real and mechanistically rich phenomenon in animal models, where gut microbes demonstrably influence brain chemistry and behaviour. In humans the picture is consistent with, but far from proof of, a causal role for the microbiome in mental health. The associations are reproducible, the mechanisms plausible, and a few intervention signals are encouraging, yet the human evidence remains predominantly correlational and methodologically uneven, and the clinical case is unproven. The honest summary is that this is a promising field that has not yet delivered a validated clinical application, and that its credibility depends on resisting the temptation to oversell. Careful longitudinal and interventional work, standardised methods and a sober distinction between what microbes can do and what they do do will determine whether the gut-brain axis becomes a pillar of psychiatry or a cautionary tale about correlation mistaken for cause.

# A Fresh Start for the Nation's Finances: Abolishing Income Tax and Adopting a Single Flat Consumption Tax

## Executive Summary

The income tax is a relic of a bygone age. It is complicated, intrusive and punishing, and it taxes the one thing a healthy economy needs most: work. This white paper sets out a bold and simple alternative. We propose abolishing the federal income tax in its entirety, along with payroll taxes, capital gains taxes and the estate tax, and replacing the whole edifice with a single flat consumption tax levied on retail sales. The plan is simple enough to explain on a postcard, fair enough that everyone pays the same rate, and powerful enough to unleash a wave of growth, savings and prosperity. The time for half-measures has passed. The nation deserves a tax system worthy of a free people.

## 1. The Problem with the Income Tax

Few institutions are as universally loathed as the income tax. Citizens spend billions of hours and billions of dollars every year simply trying to comply with it. The tax code runs to many thousands of pages, an impenetrable thicket of brackets, deductions, credits, phase-outs and exemptions that no ordinary person can hope to understand. An entire industry of accountants, lawyers and lobbyists exists only to navigate, exploit and perpetuate this complexity.

Worse, the income tax punishes exactly the behaviour a prosperous society should reward. Every additional hour worked, every promotion earned, every business expanded is met by the taxman's hand reaching deeper into the citizen's pocket. The income tax is, quite literally, a tax on productivity. It discourages effort, it discourages investment, and it discourages the saving on which all future growth depends. A system that penalises work and thrift is a system designed for stagnation.

The income tax is also an instrument of surveillance. To enforce it, the government must know what every citizen earns, from whom, and how. It must track wages, dividends, interest, capital gains and gifts. This is an extraordinary intrusion into private life, one we have come to accept only through long habituation. A free people should not have to file an annual confession of their financial affairs to the state.

## 2. The Solution: A Single Flat Consumption Tax

Our proposal is elegant in its simplicity. Abolish the income tax. Abolish the payroll tax. Abolish the capital gains tax and the estate tax. In their place, levy a single flat tax on the final retail sale of goods and services. Every purchase is taxed once, at the same rate, with no exceptions and no loopholes.

The advantages are immediate and obvious.

**Simplicity.** The plan can be described on a postcard. There are no brackets, no deductions, no credits, no annual filing for individuals. Citizens would never again fill out a tax return. The thousands of pages of the tax code would be replaced by a single rate.

**Fairness.** Everyone pays the same rate on what they spend. There is no special treatment for the well-connected, no carve-outs for favoured industries, no army of lobbyists carving loopholes into the code. The billionaire and the bus driver pay the identical rate at the till. What could be fairer than that?

**Growth.** By removing the tax on work, saving and investment, the plan would unleash the productive energies of the nation. People would keep their entire pay cheque. Businesses would invest without the distorting drag of the corporate and capital gains taxes. Savings would surge, because saving would no longer be punished. Economists have long agreed that consumption taxes are more pro-growth than income taxes, and the logic is undeniable.

These objections, examined honestly, dissolve on contact with the facts. The case against reform is a case for the indefensible status quo. The administrative simplicity of the new system would also free up resources currently consumed by enforcement of the old one. We are confident that a determined government could complete the transition within a single decade, leaving behind a tax system fit for the century ahead.

Concerns about those who have already paid income tax on savings that they will now spend under a consumption tax, and who might feel taxed twice, can be addressed with sensible transitional reliefs. The details are technical and need not detain us here; the point is that no genuine obstacle stands between the nation and this superior system, only a failure of nerve.

We can do better, and the path is clear. A single flat consumption tax would be simple, fair, pro-growth and respectful of liberty. We urge lawmakers to seize the moment, abolish the income tax, and give the country the simple, fair and growth-friendly tax system that a free and ambitious people deserve. The postcard is ready. All that is needed is the courage to mail it.

Few institutions are as universally loathed as the income tax. Citizens spend billions of hours and billions of dollars every year simply trying to comply with it. The tax code runs to many thousands of pages, an impenetrable thicket of brackets, deductions, credits, phase-outs and exemptions that no ordinary person can hope to understand. An entire industry of accountants, lawyers and lobbyists exists only to navigate, exploit and perpetuate this complexity.

Worse, the income tax punishes exactly the behaviour a prosperous society should reward. Every additional hour worked, every promotion earned, every business expanded is met by the taxman's hand reaching deeper into the citizen's pocket. The income tax is, quite literally, a tax on productivity. It discourages effort, it discourages investment, and it discourages the saving on which all future growth depends. A system that penalises work and thrift is a system designed for stagnation.

The income tax is also an instrument of surveillance. To enforce it, the government must know what every citizen earns, from whom, and how. It must track wages, dividends, interest, capital gains and gifts. This is an extraordinary intrusion into private life, one we have come to accept only through long habituation. A free people should not have to file an annual confession of their financial affairs to the state.

Our proposal is elegant in its simplicity. Abolish the income tax. Abolish the payroll tax. Abolish the capital gains tax and the estate tax. **Fairness.** Everyone pays the same rate on what they spend. There is no special treatment for the well-connected, no carve-outs for favoured industries, no army of lobbyists carving loopholes into the code. The billionaire and the bus driver pay the identical rate at the till. What could be fairer than that?

**Growth.** By removing the tax on work, saving and investment, the plan would unleash the productive energies of the nation. People would keep their entire pay cheque. Businesses would invest without the distorting drag of the corporate and capital gains taxes. Savings would surge, because saving would no longer be punished. Economists have long agreed that consumption taxes are more pro-growth than income taxes, and the logic is undeniable.

**Freedom.** The government would no longer need to know what anyone earns. The surveillance apparatus of the income tax could be dismantled. The relationship between citizen and state would be transformed from one of suspicion to one of trust.

Some will object that a flat rate is unfair because it does not rise with income. This objection rests on a confusion. Fairness does not mean treating people differently; it means treating them the same. A flat consumption tax does exactly that. Everyone faces the identical rate. The person who spends more, pays more, automatically and in proportion. A wealthy family that buys a yacht pays vastly more tax than a young couple buying groceries, without any need for brackets or means-testing. The tax is therefore progressive in its effect while remaining beautifully simple in its design.

Indeed, the flat rate is the only truly equal tax. Graduated income taxes single out the successful for higher rates, which is a form of punishment for achievement. A flat consumption tax treats every citizen as an equal before the law of taxation, exactly as a just society should.

## 4. Unleashing Economic Growth

The growth case for this reform is overwhelming. Consider the incentives. Under the income tax, the reward for extra work is reduced by the marginal rate. Under a pure consumption tax, work is not taxed at all; only spending is. The incentive to earn is fully restored.

The same logic applies to saving and investment. The income tax taxes the return on savings, so it penalises the patient and rewards the spendthrift. A consumption tax does the opposite: money that is saved and invested is never taxed until it is finally spent, if it ever is. This is precisely the incentive structure a growing economy needs. Nations that save and invest grow; nations that consume and borrow stagnate. Our plan rebuilds the foundations of long-term prosperity.

Capital would also flood into the country. With no income tax, no capital gains tax and no corporate tax, the nation would become the most attractive destination for investment in the world. Factories, headquarters and entrepreneurs would relocate to take advantage of the most favourable tax environment anywhere. The resulting boom in jobs and wages would lift every citizen.

The historical record supports optimism. Periods of lower taxation have generally coincided with stronger growth, and the most dynamic economies tend to be those that tax consumption rather than income. The direction of the evidence is clear, and it points squarely towards our proposal.

A natural question is what rate would be required to replace the revenue currently raised by the income tax. The answer is reassuringly modest. Because the consumption base is broad, covering nearly all spending in the economy, even a single-digit-into-low-double-digit rate would raise enormous sums. Once the growth effects of the reform take hold, the expanding economy would generate still more revenue at any given rate, allowing the rate itself to fall over time. Critics will raise objections. Let us dispatch the main ones.

*It will hurt the poor.* On the contrary. The poor currently bear the hidden weight of payroll taxes and the embedded cost of corporate taxes passed on in higher prices. Abolish those, and prices for many goods would actually fall. The poor would also keep their entire pay cheque, with nothing withheld. They would be among the biggest winners.

*It cannot raise enough revenue.* This worry ignores the breadth of the consumption base and the growth dividend described above. A broad base at a moderate rate raises ample revenue, and a growing economy raises more.

*People will evade it.* Every tax invites some evasion, but a single-rate retail tax is far simpler to administer than the labyrinthine income tax, with its endless opportunities for avoidance through deductions and shelters. Simplicity is the enemy of evasion.

*The transition will be disruptive.* Any reform involves change, but the destination is so superior that temporary adjustment is a price well worth paying. Bold reforms are never achieved by those who fear the first step.

*It concentrates too much power in a single rate.* Some worry that relying on one tax makes revenue volatile or gives politicians a single dial to abuse. But a single visible rate is in fact the best discipline of all: when every citizen pays the same posted rate at the till, any attempt to raise it is felt immediately and universally, which makes increases politically costly and therefore rare. Compare that with the income tax, where rates can be nudged upward through obscure changes to brackets and deductions that few notice. Transparency is a safeguard, not a danger.

These objections, examined honestly, dissolve on contact with the facts. The case against reform is a case for the indefensible status quo. Every one of these worries assumes that the present system works tolerably well and that change is the thing to be feared. The truth is the reverse: it is the status quo that is failing the nation every single day, quietly and expensively, and it is reform that offers relief. The burden of proof lies not with those who would fix a broken system but with those who would defend it.

## 7. The Burden of the Current System in Detail

It is worth dwelling on just how heavy the present system is, because familiarity has bred acceptance of the intolerable. Consider first the sheer scale of compliance. The hours that citizens and businesses devote each year to record-keeping, form-filling and the hiring of professionals represent an enormous deadweight loss, productive time and money diverted into the unproductive task of working out what one owes. None of this effort builds a road, teaches a child or invents a product. It exists solely to feed the machinery of the income tax.

People are pushed towards debt, because interest is treated favourably, and away from saving, because returns are taxed. Firms structure themselves around the tax code rather than around what makes commercial sense. Whole categories of economic decision are warped by the desire to minimise tax rather than to maximise genuine value. A clean consumption tax, falling on all final sales at one rate, would remove these distortions at a stroke. The market, not the tax accountant, would once again allocate capital.

Consider, finally, the corrosive effect on civic trust. A code so complex that no citizen can understand it, so riddled with special provisions that the well-advised pay less than the honest, breeds cynicism about government itself. People reasonably suspect that the system is rigged in favour of those who can afford the cleverest advisers. A single, transparent rate that everyone can see and understand would do more to restore faith in the fairness of government than a thousand pious speeches. Simplicity is not merely an administrative convenience; it is a democratic virtue.

These burdens are not abstractions. They fall on every household and every business, every year, and they compound over a lifetime. A reform that lifted them would be among the most consequential improvements in the daily life of citizens that any government could deliver. That alone should command the attention of every serious lawmaker.

## 8. International Lessons

The world offers encouraging examples of the direction we propose. Across the developed world, governments have come to rely heavily on broad-based consumption taxes, recognising their efficiency and their gentle treatment of saving and investment. Value-added taxes, a close cousin of our proposal, now form a pillar of public finance on every continent. The trend is unmistakable: as economies modernise, they lean ever more on taxing what people consume rather than what they earn. We propose simply to follow this logic to its clean and natural conclusion, sweeping away the income tax altogether rather than letting two systems coexist in expensive parallel.

Some jurisdictions have gone further and prospered. Places with no income tax at all have become magnets for talent, capital and enterprise. Workers flock to keep their full pay, and companies relocate to escape the punishing rates levied elsewhere. The lesson is plain. Where the income tax is light or absent, prosperity follows. Our plan would extend that advantage to the entire nation.

Critics may point out that the countries leaning on consumption taxes typically retain their income taxes too, rather than abolishing them. The fact that no large nation has yet had the courage to abolish the income tax outright is an argument for leadership, not for caution. Someone must go first, and the rewards will accrue to the bold.

## 9. A Phased Path to Implementation

A reform of this magnitude need not happen overnight, and we envisage a smooth and confident transition. In the first phase, the consumption tax would be enacted and the income tax rates would begin to fall in step, so that citizens feel the relief immediately. In the second phase, the payroll, capital gains and estate taxes would be folded into the new system. In the final phase, the income tax would be repealed entirely and its enforcement machinery wound down, returning to citizens the time and money they once spent on compliance.

Throughout the transition, the expanding economy would cushion any short-term adjustment. As growth accelerates, revenues would rise, smoothing the path and allowing fine adjustments to the rate. The administrative simplicity of the new system would also free up resources currently consumed by enforcement of the old one. We are confident that a determined government could complete the transition within a single decade, leaving behind a tax system fit for the century ahead.

Concerns about those who have already paid income tax on savings that they will now spend under a consumption tax, and who might feel taxed twice, can be addressed with sensible transitional reliefs. The details are technical and need not detain us here; the point is that no genuine obstacle stands between the nation and this superior system, only a failure of nerve.

## 10. Conclusion: The Time Is Now

The income tax has failed. It is complex, punishing, intrusive and unloved. It taxes work, penalises saving, funds an industry of compliance and turns the state into a snoop. We can do better, and the path is clear. A single flat consumption tax would be simple, fair, pro-growth and respectful of liberty. It would let citizens keep what they earn, reward thrift, attract investment from around the world and restore trust between the people and their government.

This is not a timid proposal, and it is not meant to be. The nation faces a choice between a discredited past and a prosperous future. We urge lawmakers to seize the moment, abolish the income tax, and give the country the simple, fair and growth-friendly tax system that a free and ambitious people deserve. The postcard is ready. All that is needed is the courage to mail it.

Few institutions are as universally loathed as the income tax. Citizens spend billions of hours and billions of dollars every year simply trying to comply with it. An entire industry of accountants, lawyers and lobbyists exists only to navigate, exploit and perpetuate this complexity.

Worse, the income tax punishes exactly the behaviour a prosperous society should reward. Every additional hour worked, every promotion earned, every business expanded is met by the taxman's hand reaching deeper into the citizen's pocket. The income tax is, quite literally, a tax on productivity. It discourages effort, it discourages investment, and it discourages the saving on which all future growth depends. A system that penalises work and thrift is a system designed for stagnation.

The income tax is also an instrument of surveillance. To enforce it, the government must know what every citizen earns, from whom, and how. It must track wages, dividends, interest, capital gains and gifts. This is an extraordinary intrusion into private life, one we have come to accept only through long habituation. A free people should not have to file an annual confession of their financial affairs to the state.

Our proposal is elegant in its simplicity. Abolish the income tax. Abolish the payroll tax. Abolish the capital gains tax and the estate tax. In their place, levy a single flat tax on the final retail sale of goods and services. Every purchase is taxed once, at the same rate, with no exceptions and no loopholes.

**Fairness.** Everyone pays the same rate on what they spend. There is no special treatment for the well-connected, no carve-outs for favoured industries, no army of lobbyists carving loopholes into the code. The billionaire and the bus driver pay the identical rate at the till. What could be fairer than that?

Businesses would invest without the distorting drag of the corporate and capital gains taxes. Savings would surge, because saving would no longer be punished. Some will object that a flat rate is unfair because it does not rise with income. This objection rests on a confusion. Fairness does not mean treating people differently; it means treating them the same. A flat consumption tax does exactly that. Everyone faces the identical rate. The person who spends more, pays more, automatically and in proportion. A wealthy family that buys a yacht pays vastly more tax than a young couple buying groceries, without any need for brackets or means-testing. The tax is therefore progressive in its effect while remaining beautifully simple in its design.

Indeed, the flat rate is the only truly equal tax. Graduated income taxes single out the successful for higher rates, which is a form of punishment for achievement. A flat consumption tax treats every citizen as an equal before the law of taxation, exactly as a just society should.

The same logic applies to saving and investment. The income tax taxes the return on savings, so it penalises the patient and rewards the spendthrift. A consumption tax does the opposite: money that is saved and invested is never taxed until it is finally spent, if it ever is. This is precisely the incentive structure a growing economy needs. Nations that save and invest grow; nations that consume and borrow stagnate. Our plan rebuilds the foundations of long-term prosperity.

Capital would also flood into the country. With no income tax, no capital gains tax and no corporate tax, the nation would become the most attractive destination for investment in the world. Factories, headquarters and entrepreneurs would relocate to take advantage of the most favourable tax environment anywhere. The resulting boom in jobs and wages would lift every citizen.

A natural question is what rate would be required to replace the revenue currently raised by the income tax. The answer is reassuringly modest. Because the consumption base is broad, covering nearly all spending in the economy, even a single-digit-into-low-double-digit rate would raise enormous sums. Once the growth effects of the reform take hold, the expanding economy would generate still more revenue at any given rate, allowing the rate itself to fall over time. A tax system that becomes cheaper as the economy grows is a virtuous circle that the income tax could never achieve.

We are confident that a moderate flat rate would fully fund the legitimate functions of government while leaving citizens far better off than they are today. The exact figure can be settled by technical experts during implementation; the principle is what matters, and the principle is sound.

Critics will raise objections. Let us dispatch the main ones.

*It will hurt the poor.* On the contrary. The poor currently bear the hidden weight of payroll taxes and the embedded cost of corporate taxes passed on in higher prices. We are confident that a determined government could complete the transition within a single decade, leaving behind a tax system fit for the century ahead.

We urge lawmakers to seize the moment, abolish the income tax, and give the country the simple, fair and growth-friendly tax system that a free and ambitious people deserve. The postcard is ready. Every additional hour worked, every promotion earned, every business expanded is met by the taxman's hand reaching deeper into the citizen's pocket. A system that penalises work and thrift is a system designed for stagnation.

The income tax is also an instrument of surveillance. To enforce it, the government must know what every citizen earns, from whom, and how. It must track wages, dividends, interest, capital gains and gifts. This is an extraordinary intrusion into private life, one we have come to accept only through long habituation. A free people should not have to file an annual confession of their financial affairs to the state.

Our proposal is elegant in its simplicity. Abolish the income tax. Abolish the payroll tax. Abolish the capital gains tax and the estate tax. **Fairness.** Everyone pays the same rate on what they spend. There is no special treatment for the well-connected, no carve-outs for favoured industries, no army of lobbyists carving loopholes into the code. The billionaire and the bus driver pay the identical rate at the till. What could be fairer than that?

**Growth.** By removing the tax on work, saving and investment, the plan would unleash the productive energies of the nation. People would keep their entire pay cheque. Businesses would invest without the distorting drag of the corporate and capital gains taxes. Savings would surge, because saving would no longer be punished. Economists have long agreed that consumption taxes are more pro-growth than income taxes, and the logic is undeniable.

**Freedom.** The government would no longer need to know what anyone earns. The surveillance apparatus of the income tax could be dismantled. The relationship between citizen and state would be transformed from one of suspicion to one of trust.

Some will object that a flat rate is unfair because it does not rise with income. This objection rests on a confusion. Fairness does not mean treating people differently; it means treating them the same. A flat consumption tax does exactly that. Everyone faces the identical rate. The person who spends more, pays more, automatically and in proportion. A wealthy family that buys a yacht pays vastly more tax than a young couple buying groceries, without any need for brackets or means-testing. The tax is therefore progressive in its effect while remaining beautifully simple in its design.

Indeed, the flat rate is the only truly equal tax. Graduated income taxes single out the successful for higher rates, which is a form of punishment for achievement. A flat consumption tax treats every citizen as an equal before the law of taxation, exactly as a just society should.

## 4. Unleashing Economic Growth

The growth case for this reform is overwhelming. Consider the incentives. Under the income tax, the reward for extra work is reduced by the marginal rate. Under a pure consumption tax, work is not taxed at all; only spending is. The incentive to earn is fully restored.

The same logic applies to saving and investment. The income tax taxes the return on savings, so it penalises the patient and rewards the spendthrift. A consumption tax does the opposite: money that is saved and invested is never taxed until it is finally spent, if it ever is. This is precisely the incentive structure a growing economy needs. Nations that save and invest grow; nations that consume and borrow stagnate. Our plan rebuilds the foundations of long-term prosperity.

Capital would also flood into the country. With no income tax, no capital gains tax and no corporate tax, the nation would become the most attractive destination for investment in the world. Factories, headquarters and entrepreneurs would relocate to take advantage of the most favourable tax environment anywhere. The resulting boom in jobs and wages would lift every citizen.

A natural question is what rate would be required to replace the revenue currently raised by the income tax. The answer is reassuringly modest. Because the consumption base is broad, covering nearly all spending in the economy, even a single-digit-into-low-double-digit rate would raise enormous sums. Critics will raise objections. Let us dispatch the main ones.

*It will hurt the poor.* On the contrary. The poor currently bear the hidden weight of payroll taxes and the embedded cost of corporate taxes passed on in higher prices. Abolish those, and prices for many goods would actually fall. The poor would also keep their entire pay cheque, with nothing withheld. They would be among the biggest winners.

*It cannot raise enough revenue.* This worry ignores the breadth of the consumption base and the growth dividend described above. A broad base at a moderate rate raises ample revenue, and a growing economy raises more.

*People will evade it.* Every tax invites some evasion, but a single-rate retail tax is far simpler to administer than the labyrinthine income tax, with its endless opportunities for avoidance through deductions and shelters. Simplicity is the enemy of evasion.

*The transition will be disruptive.* Any reform involves change, but the destination is so superior that temporary adjustment is a price well worth paying. Bold reforms are never achieved by those who fear the first step.

*It concentrates too much power in a single rate.* Some worry that relying on one tax makes revenue volatile or gives politicians a single dial to abuse. But a single visible rate is in fact the best discipline of all: when every citizen pays the same posted rate at the till, any attempt to raise it is felt immediately and universally, which makes increases politically costly and therefore rare. Compare that with the income tax, where rates can be nudged upward through obscure changes to brackets and deductions that few notice. Transparency is a safeguard, not a danger.

These objections, examined honestly, dissolve on contact with the facts. The case against reform is a case for the indefensible status quo. Every one of these worries assumes that the present system works tolerably well and that change is the thing to be feared. The truth is the reverse: it is the status quo that is failing the nation every single day, quietly and expensively, and it is reform that offers relief. The burden of proof lies not with those who would fix a broken system but with those who would defend it.

## 7. The Burden of the Current System in Detail

It is worth dwelling on just how heavy the present system is, because familiarity has bred acceptance of the intolerable. Consider first the sheer scale of compliance. The hours that citizens and businesses devote each year to record-keeping, form-filling and the hiring of professionals represent an enormous deadweight loss, productive time and money diverted into the unproductive task of working out what one owes. None of this effort builds a road, teaches a child or invents a product. It exists solely to feed the machinery of the income tax.

People are pushed towards debt, because interest is treated favourably, and away from saving, because returns are taxed. Firms structure themselves around the tax code rather than around what makes commercial sense. Whole categories of economic decision are warped by the desire to minimise tax rather than to maximise genuine value. A clean consumption tax, falling on all final sales at one rate, would remove these distortions at a stroke. The market, not the tax accountant, would once again allocate capital.

Consider, finally, the corrosive effect on civic trust. A code so complex that no citizen can understand it, so riddled with special provisions that the well-advised pay less than the honest, breeds cynicism about government itself. People reasonably suspect that the system is rigged in favour of those who can afford the cleverest advisers. A single, transparent rate that everyone can see and understand would do more to restore faith in the fairness of government than a thousand pious speeches. Simplicity is not merely an administrative convenience; it is a democratic virtue.

These burdens are not abstractions. They fall on every household and every business, every year, and they compound over a lifetime. A reform that lifted them would be among the most consequential improvements in the daily life of citizens that any government could deliver. That alone should command the attention of every serious lawmaker.

## 8. International Lessons

The world offers encouraging examples of the direction we propose. Across the developed world, governments have come to rely heavily on broad-based consumption taxes, recognising their efficiency and their gentle treatment of saving and investment. Value-added taxes, a close cousin of our proposal, now form a pillar of public finance on every continent. The trend is unmistakable: as economies modernise, they lean ever more on taxing what people consume rather than what they earn. We propose simply to follow this logic to its clean and natural conclusion, sweeping away the income tax altogether rather than letting two systems coexist in expensive parallel.

Some jurisdictions have gone further and prospered. Places with no income tax at all have become magnets for talent, capital and enterprise. Workers flock to keep their full pay, and companies relocate to escape the punishing rates levied elsewhere. The lesson is plain. Where the income tax is light or absent, prosperity follows. Our plan would extend that advantage to the entire nation.

The fact that no large nation has yet had the courage to abolish the income tax outright is an argument for leadership, not for caution. Someone must go first, and the rewards will accrue to the bold.

## 9. A Phased Path to Implementation

A reform of this magnitude need not happen overnight, and we envisage a smooth and confident transition. In the first phase, the consumption tax would be enacted and the income tax rates would begin to fall in step, so that citizens feel the relief immediately. In the second phase, the payroll, capital gains and estate taxes would be folded into the new system. In the final phase, the income tax would be repealed entirely and its enforcement machinery wound down, returning to citizens the time and money they once spent on compliance.

Throughout the transition, the expanding economy would cushion any short-term adjustment. As growth accelerates, revenues would rise, smoothing the path and allowing fine adjustments to the rate. The administrative simplicity of the new system would also free up resources currently consumed by enforcement of the old one. We are confident that a determined government could complete the transition within a single decade, leaving behind a tax system fit for the century ahead.

Concerns about those who have already paid income tax on savings that they will now spend under a consumption tax, and who might feel taxed twice, can be addressed with sensible transitional reliefs. The details are technical and need not detain us here; the point is that no genuine obstacle stands between the nation and this superior system, only a failure of nerve.

## 10. Conclusion: The Time Is Now

The income tax has failed. It is complex, punishing, intrusive and unloved. It taxes work, penalises saving, funds an industry of compliance and turns the state into a snoop. We can do better, and the path is clear. A single flat consumption tax would be simple, fair, pro-growth and respectful of liberty. It would let citizens keep what they earn, reward thrift, attract investment from around the world and restore trust between the people and their government.

This is not a timid proposal, and it is not meant to be. The nation faces a choice between a discredited past and a prosperous future. We urge lawmakers to seize the moment, abolish the income tax, and give the country the simple, fair and growth-friendly tax system that a free and ambitious people deserve. The postcard is ready. All that is needed is the courage to mail it.

We can do better, and the path is clear. A single flat consumption tax would be simple, fair, pro-growth and respectful of liberty. This is not a timid proposal, and it is not meant to be. The nation faces a choice between a discredited past and a prosperous future. We urge lawmakers to seize the moment, abolish the income tax, and give the country the simple, fair and growth-friendly tax system that a free and ambitious people deserve. The postcard is ready. All that is needed is the courage to mail it.
